stem: A client has life-threatening obstetric hemorrhage and the facility’s massive transfusion protocol (MTP) is activated. Which statement by the nurse is most accurate?

options.A: The MTP supports rapid, coordinated delivery of red blood cells and other indicated blood components such as plasma and platelets according to the facility protocol while ongoing clinical and laboratory findings guide resuscitation.
options.B: Every obstetric MTP must use exactly the same 1:1:1 red-cell-to-plasma-to-platelet ratio because one universal ratio has been proven superior in obstetric hemorrhage.
options.C: An MTP provides crystalloid fluid only and is not intended to facilitate rapid blood-component support.
options.D: Massive transfusion protocols are limited to trauma care and should not be used for severe obstetric hemorrhage.

rationale: A is correct. AABB’s current massive-transfusion guidance supports organized protocols that enable transfusion services to provide blood components rapidly during massive hemorrhage. ACOG also recommends access to massive transfusion capability for severe obstetric hemorrhage and describes rapid replacement with red blood cells, plasma, and platelets while clinical and laboratory data guide care. Importantly, ACOG notes that controlled studies have not established one best blood-product ratio for obstetric hemorrhage, so B overstates the evidence. C and D misrepresent the purpose and obstetric applicability of MTPs.
educational_objective: Understand that an obstetric MTP enables rapid, coordinated multi-component blood-product resuscitation according to institutional protocol and evolving clinical/laboratory needs rather than requiring one universal component ratio.
source_organization: Association for the Advancement of Blood & Biotherapies (AABB); American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists
source_document_title: AABB Guide to Massive Transfusion; Placenta Accreta Spectrum; Postpartum Hemorrhage Practice Bulletin
source_version_date: AABB Guide 2023; ACOG Placenta Accreta Spectrum current as accessed 2026-08-17; Postpartum Hemorrhage PB reaffirmed 2024 with July 2025 update
source_locator: AABB Guide to Massive Transfusion — best practices/regulatory requirements for establishing and operating massive transfusion or massive hemorrhage protocols. ACOG Placenta Accreta Spectrum — blood bank capable of massive transfusion protocols; rapid transfusion of packed red cells, plasma, and platelets; no controlled studies establish the best blood-product ratio in obstetrics; laboratory and clinical data inform replacement
source_claim_supported: Massive transfusion protocols provide organized rapid access to multiple blood components during severe hemorrhage, including obstetric hemorrhage; component ratios are protocol- and situation-dependent because one universally superior obstetric ratio has not been established.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing
blueprint_locator: Physiological Integrity — Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies; administer blood and blood products safely, monitor transfusion therapy, and coordinate parenteral resuscitation
blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — massive transfusion protocol in obstetric hemorrhage
correction_summary: Rebuilt the source item to remove the implication that all massive transfusion protocols use one predetermined universal blood-product ratio. The final version tests the evidence-supported function of an MTP—rapid coordinated multi-component transfusion—while preserving institution-specific protocols and ongoing clinical/laboratory guidance. Category corrected from infection control to Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies.
audit_reviewer: OpenAI GPT-5.6 Sol — Rule 1 clinical audit + adversarial second pass

audit_findings.clinical_category: massive transfusion / obstetric hemorrhage / blood components
audit_findings.source_audit: Verified against AABB’s 2023 Guide to Massive Transfusion and current ACOG obstetric hemorrhage material. Both support massive transfusion capability; ACOG explicitly states that the best component ratio in obstetrics has not been established by controlled studies.
audit_findings.claim_by_claim: A describes rapid multi-component support without specifying a universal ratio or transfusion trigger. It also allows clinical/laboratory data to guide ongoing resuscitation rather than implying a fixed sequence is always sufficient.
audit_findings.choice_A: Correct; it accurately describes the purpose and flexible evidence-based use of an obstetric MTP.
audit_findings.choice_B: Incorrect; one universally superior obstetric 1:1:1 ratio has not been established.
audit_findings.choice_C: Incorrect; MTPs are designed to facilitate blood-component resuscitation, not crystalloid alone.
audit_findings.choice_D: Incorrect; massive transfusion protocols are relevant to severe obstetric hemorrhage as well as trauma and other causes of massive bleeding.
audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only A captures both the rapid blood-component function and the absence of a universal obstetric ratio requirement.
audit_findings.cueing: All options address what an MTP provides and how it is applied during massive hemorrhage.
audit_findings.blueprint: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies is appropriate because the central construct is safe, coordinated administration of blood products during resuscitation.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: Rechecked AABB source authority, obstetric applicability, fixed-ratio evidence limits, blood-component scope, clinical/lab guidance, category mapping, and second-answer risk. No unresolved conflict remained.
